findings.title: Salesforce token refresh references prisma without importing it
findings.body: The new refresh path calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` at this line, but the file does not import `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. TypeScript will fail to compile with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, blocking the build.

findings.title: Minimum token schema uses literal computed keys instead of wildcards
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` is evaluated once to a fixed property name (for example `ZodString`), not a wildcard for arbitrary token fields. In credential-sharing mode `minimumTokenResponseSchema` therefore requires a numeric property with that literal name and normal OAuth token responses fail validation; because the schema is not a passthrough, valid fields such as `expires_in` and `refresh_token` are also stripped. This breaks token refresh for Google, Office 365, Salesforce, and Zoom whenever sync is enabled.

findings.title: Missing refresh tokens are replaced with the literal string refresh_token
findings.body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, this code writes the literal value `refresh_token` into the result. Callers such as Office365Calendar spread the parsed data over the existing credential, so a response without a new refresh token overwrites a valid stored refresh token with that placeholder. A later refresh using the placeholder will fail and disconnect the integration. The old refresh token should be preserved instead.

findings.title: Google refresh reads `.data` from a fetch Response in sync mode
findings.body: With credential sharing enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `Response` from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. This code reads `res?.data` and then `token.access_token`/`token.expiry_date`, which are undefined on a Response. The refresh throws, is swallowed by the catch block, and Google API calls continue with expired credentials.

findings.title: Google stores the SafeParseReturnType wrapper as the credential key
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the `safeParse` result object `{ success, data }`, not the parsed token object. This line stores that wrapper directly in `prisma.credential.update`, so the credential key becomes `{ success: true, data: ... }` and no longer matches `googleCredentialSchema`. The next initialization of GoogleCalendarService will fail to parse the stored credential.

findings.title: HubSpot treats a fetch Response as a HubspotToken in sync mode
findings.body: In credential-sharing mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch `Response`, but the result is cast to `HubspotToken` and then read as `expiresIn` and `accessToken`. Those fields are undefined, so `expiryDate` becomes `NaN`, the Response object is written as the credential key, and `setAccessToken(undefined)` is called. HubSpot API calls fail and the stored credential is corrupted whenever sync is enabled.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin sends credential id as calcomUserId to the sync endpoint
findings.body: The third argument of `refreshOAuthTokens` is the Cal.com user id and is sent as `calcomUserId` to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. This call passes `credentialId` instead of `credential.userId`, so the self-hosted app store is asked to refresh tokens for a credential id as if it were a user id. The wrong user's tokens may be returned or the lookup may fail.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin treats a fetch Response as an axios response
findings.body: In credential-sharing mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch `Response`, which has no `.data` property. This line accesses `tokenInfo.data.error`, so refresh throws a TypeError and no token is stored. The local axios path works only when sharing is disabled.

findings.title: Zoho CRM treats a fetch Response as an axios response
findings.body: In credential-sharing mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch `Response`, not an axios response. `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data` is undefined here, so `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` throws and Zoho CRM token refresh fails whenever credential sync is enabled.

findings.title: Salesforce connection is built with the stale access token after refresh
findings.body: The new refresh code fetches and stores a new access token at lines 75-99, but the returned `jsforce.Connection` still uses `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` from the old credential. If the old access token was expired, the current operation fails even though a valid token was just saved in the database. It should use the refreshed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED stores the encryption key instead of a boolean
findings.body: `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` returns the encryption key string when both env vars are set. The exported constant is therefore a secret, not an enabled flag. If it is logged, serialized, or imported into code that reaches the client, `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` can leak. Use `Boolean(...)` and keep the key out of exported constants.

findings.title: Credential-mutating webhook accepts any HTTP method
findings.body: The handler never checks `req.method`; it will process GET, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests as long as the secret header and body are present. A credential-mutating webhook should accept only POST and return 405 for other methods.

findings.title: Updating synced credentials leaves the invalid flag set
findings.body: When a credential already exists, the update only changes `key`. If that credential was previously marked `invalid` after a refresh failure, it stays invalid and Cal.com will continue ignoring the fresh credentials from the app store. Synced credentials should reset `invalid` to false.

findings.title: Salesforce bypasses the configured credential sync endpoint
findings.body: Unlike the other integrations changed in this PR, Salesforce never calls `refreshOAuthTokens`; it always fetches directly from `login.salesforce.com` using local consumer keys. Consequently, when a self-hoster configures `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` and expects their app store to be the source of truth, Salesforce token refreshes still use Cal.com's local app secrets and never contact the app store.

findings.title: No tests cover the new credential webhook or token-sharing helpers
findings.body: This PR adds a security-sensitive endpoint that writes third-party credentials and changes token refresh paths for many integrations, but no automated tests were added. Tests are needed for bad/missing webhook secrets, non-POST methods, malformed encrypted payloads, and the different expected refresh response shapes, since simple tests would catch the response-shape and parsing failures in this change.
